column2: On the authority of Abū Masʿūd ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmr al-Anṣārī al-Badrī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Among the words that people have received from the earliest prophethood is: If you feel no shame, then do as you wish.” Reported by al-Bukhārī.

Adraka al-nās (“people have received”): they inherited it generation after generation. Al-nās is in the nominative, with the pronoun referring back to mā omitted; it may also be in the accusative, with the referring pronoun being the subject.
“From the earliest prophethood”: that which came before our Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ.
What is meant is that it is something on which the laws agree, since it came in the first of them and the rest followed in succession upon it.

Idhā lam tastaḥi (“if you feel no shame”): from ḥayāʾ (modesty), a trait that urges doing what is fine and leaving what is ugly, and prevents falling short in what is due. As for what results in failing in what is due, that is not modesty in the sense of the Sharīʿah; it is rather weakness and feebleness.

“Then do as you wish”: there are three views on this command. The first is that it has the meaning of a statement, as if he were saying: if modesty does not hold you back, you will do whatever you wish, that is, the ugly things your soul calls you to.

The second is that it is a threat, like the saying of the Exalted, “Do whatever you wish” [Fuṣṣilat 41:40]. The third is that it expresses permission: look at the deed you want to do; if it is something one need not be ashamed of, do it, and otherwise do not.
The nobility of modesty: there is no prophet who did not urge it. It was not abrogated among what was abrogated of the laws of the prophets, nor changed among what was changed of them,
because it is something whose rightness is known and whose virtue is evident, and minds agree that it is good; and whatever is like that is not abrogated.
It is modesty that restrains a person and deters him from committing evil; if he rejects it and throws off its yoke, he is like one commanded to commit every error and engage in every evil.
The printed text reads قد على صوابه, evidently for قد عُلم صوابه (“whose rightness is known”).
